title: Bartholomew (24 August)
hook: the apostle often identified with Nathanael, a man without guile

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Queenship of Mary, honored as queen because she is the mother of the King. Your line was queen and mother. Who did you ask for yesterday? Day one thousand eighteen.

"Can any thing of good come from Nazareth?" Those are the first words Nathanael says about Jesus, before they have even met. His friend Philip has just found him with big news: we have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth. And Nathanael answers with a put-down of the man's hometown. It's a rude line. It's also completely honest. He doesn't pretend to be impressed. And Philip doesn't argue with him. He just says three words: come and see. Today, the apostle the Church keeps on the twenty-fourth of August, and the honest skeptic who may be the same man. Bartholomew.
screen: `CAN ANY THING OF GOOD COME FROM NAZARETH?` → `PHILIP DOESN'T ARGUE.` → `COME AND SEE.`

segments.voice: First, a puzzle. In the lists of the twelve apostles in Matthew, Mark and Luke, there's a Bartholomew, named right beside Philip. Those Gospels never tell a single story about him. John's Gospel never uses the name Bartholomew at all. Instead, John tells about Nathanael, brought to Jesus by Philip. So tradition puts the two together: Bartholomew and Nathanael, one man. Nobody can prove it. It's a reasoned guess, held openly, and the Church reads this very story on his feast. Now the story. Nathanael walks up, and before he can say anything, Jesus says of him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile." Guile is an old word for trickery: a hidden angle, saying one thing and meaning another. Jesus doesn't scold him for the crack about Nazareth. He names what was good in it. Here is a man with nothing hidden. Nathanael is startled: how do you know me? Jesus answers that he saw him under the fig tree, before Philip ever called him. The Gospel never says what happened under that fig tree. Whatever it was, it lands. Nathanael's doubt turns, on the spot, into faith: "Rabbi, thou art the Son of God." The man who said exactly what he thought about Nazareth now says exactly what he thinks about Jesus. Same honesty, new direction. Tradition adds more: that Bartholomew preached far from home and died a martyr, by some accounts flayed alive, which is why paintings sometimes show him holding a knife. The Gospels don't tell any of that. What they keep is one moment: an honest doubter, a friend who said come and see, and a man without guile.
screen: `BARTHOLOMEW IN THE LISTS, NATHANAEL IN JOHN.` · `NO GUILE: NOTHING HIDDEN.` · `UNDER THE FIG TREE.` · `SAME HONESTY, NEW DIRECTION.` · then, large: `AN ISRAELITE INDEED, IN WHOM THERE IS NO GUILE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: no guile. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place in your life where you've been working an angle. A compliment you didn't mean. A reason you gave that wasn't the real reason. A smile that covered something. Don't punish yourself. Just see it plainly, the way Jesus saw Nathanael under the fig tree. Then ask what it would look like with nothing hidden. If you pray, you can bring it to God just as it is. If you don't, simply hold it in the light for the sit. The bell holds the time.
Bartholomew. The apostle named beside Philip, whom tradition identifies with Nathanael, the man Jesus called without guile.
Your line: without guile. Today, try being honest all day: no small fibs, no hidden angles, no compliments you don't mean. Day one thousand eighteen.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Bartholomew, apostle, on 24 August; the Gospel read at Mass that day is the calling of Nathanael from the first chapter of John.

myth: the name Bartholomew appears in John's Gospel
John never uses it. he tells of Nathanael, and tradition joins the two.
Nathanael's first words about Jesus were a put-down of Nazareth
"can any thing of good come from Nazareth?" and Jesus still calls him a man without guile.
the Gospels tell how Bartholomew died
they don't. his preaching and martyrdom come from later tradition.

fork.setup: you're Philip. your friend sneers that nothing good comes from Nazareth. what do you say?
options: argue him down with the prophets.
drop it and go on alone.
fork.reveal: Philip doesn't argue. he says "come and see," and the doubter goes with him, and ends up calling Jesus the Son of God.

original.note: Greek: bait, a trick, deceit. in John 1:47, Nathanael is the man with none.

trapdoor: what you thought: an apostle nobody remembers anything about.
what it means: tradition joins him to Nathanael, the honest skeptic Jesus called a man without guile.
what a scholar hears: Matthew, Mark and Luke pair Bartholomew with Philip but tell no story; John tells of Nathanael with Philip but never says Bartholomew. the link is a reasoned guess.

notes: The Bartholomew–Nathanael identification is presented as tradition and a reasoned guess, not fact. Confirm.
'The Church reads this very story on his feast': the Gospel for 24 August is John 1:45–51. Confirm.
Flaying is given 'by some accounts'; places of mission (India, Armenia) left out under the claims rule.
The twelve apostles: the number comes from Matthew 10:2 ('the names of the twelve apostles'), cited as paraphrase. Confirm.
Original: δόλος in John 1:47 (ἐν ᾧ δόλος οὐκ ἔστιν). Confirm.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of John 1:46, 1:47 and 1:49.
